newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO struggles for deal to scrap infotech tariffs.
newsitem.headline: WTO struggles for deal to scrap infotech tariffs.

text.p: Trade ministers scrambled on Wednesday to reach an accord to scrap tariffs in the world's fast-growing information technology sector.
Key developed nations have targeted an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) as vital to the success of this week's gathering of the World Trade Organisation.

United States and European Union negotiators scheduled another round of meetings on the sidelines of the December 9-13 128-nation WTO ministerial conference to settle outstanding disagreements over the outline of an ITA after meeting in four closed-door sessions on Tuesday.
"There is not an agreement yet," European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said after meeting Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.
"There is agreement on many points. There are some outstanding ones. We are trying to resolve those."

The United States, with strong backing from Japan, is keen to see an accord to free up trade in the $600 billion market for computers, software chips and other high-technology products by the year 2000.

The Big Four trade powers -- the United States, the EU, Japan and Canada -- hope to settle their differences, in particular over the touchy question of product coverage, before meeting again later on Wednesday with other nations interested in joining the infotech accord.
"We are continuing to work with our Quad (Big Four) partners and with many other delegates to find a formula that will succeed," a U.S. official told reporters.

A Japanese government source told Reuters earlier that gaps still remained among the Big Four powers, particularly over product coverage. But he added: "I am hopeful we will reach a consensus before the afternoon meeting starts."

Late on Tuesday developing countries were shown a draft outline of an accord worked out by the Big Four, but the draft did not specify product coverage or spell out what sort of flexibility could be granted to developing countries on the timing of the tariff cuts, the Japanese source said.

Indonesian Trade and Industry Minister Tunky Ariwibowo told a news conference the bulk of the proposals contained in the draft outline would be acceptable but Jakarta had problems with some of the products detailed in the ITA.
These were mainly in what he called the "downstream area," meaning lower technology.
"On the upstream products and the middle stream products, we can okay (it). We will have zero tariffs by the year 2000," he said. "We can live with that with some sort of flexibility."
Singapore gave more wholehearted support, saying it supported the proposed ITA initiative.
"We stand ready to join the ITA and look forward to achieving the maximum outcome possible by the end of this meeting," Singapore Minister for Communications Mah Bow Tan told the plenary session.
Washington hopes that in addition to a broad infotech pact by as many countries as possible, the WTO will endorse the ITA deal in its Ministerial Declaration on Friday.
That would allow WTO members unable to sign on now to do so at a later date by presenting revised tariff schedules at the WTO in Geneva, the U.S. official said.
